title: From Postgres to ClickHouse and Back: Building a Unified OLTP + OLAP Database for AI Workloads

segments.text: I'm Kaushik. I lead the managed Postgres
efforts at ClickHouse.
Um today I wanted to talk about a
pattern that we are seeing emerge a lot
with our users, which is using Postgres
plus for transactions and ClickHouse for
analytics, and how these two together
make a unified data stack.
So, I want to cover what we are seeing
and where the customers are using this
pattern,
what gaps exist in this pattern, how we
are trying to overcome some of these
gaps, and what the general shift these
days has been.
So, before we go too deep into this, I
wanted to set the stage and give some
context around my background.
So, I started PeerDB, a Y Combinator
company, in 2023.
The goal was simple,
to make data movement out of Postgres as
seamless as possible.
I've seen this pattern emerge
throughout my career. So, I used to work
at Palantir and Google after this,
and um
moving data out of Postgres was always a
challenge, right? It was not a challenge
as much when your data size is like 5 to
10 GB, but once you start hitting
hundreds of gigabytes and terabytes,
it's a very fragile process. So, we
built a company around this. We were
moving data from Postgres into queues,
into storage, into OLAP databases like
and data warehouses like Snowflake,
BigQuery ClickHouse.
In 2024, we got acquired by ClickHouse
because we saw tremendous amount of
momentum in users moving data from
Postgres to ClickHouse. Right? Um
I'll talk a little bit about the pattern

managed Postgres offering within
ClickHouse. Right?

familiar with both these databases, but
I wanted to spend a couple of minutes
giving a quick background about these as
well.

used database in today's market. There's
even a saying that goes around, "Use
Postgres for everything."
Uh this talk kind of disagrees with
that, but you get the premise, right?
Like Postgres is so universal, it's good
at a lot of things. It has support for
extensions that let you add on to the
existing functionality of Postgres and
do more things with it. So, it's great
for row-based lookups and row-based
operations. It's great for transactions,
and it has all the asset guarantees, as
well.
And on the other other side, you have
ClickHouse, um which is great for
real-time analytics. OLAP is the bread
and butter, right? So, it's a columnar
database. It's fundamentally different
from how Postgres stores data.
It trades off transactionality
for great performance in ingestion, in
in roll-up queries. It has refreshable
materialized views, etc.
And um yeah, both of these are very
different tools. They're great at what
they do, and they're great at these
cases, but they share the same
underlying ethos of being open-source
first.

trying to cover earlier, right? So, when
Pganalyze got acquired by ClickHouse, I
had the intuition that Postgres plus
ClickHouse was going to be a very
powerful combination,

users using this pattern, just among the
ones that we've observed, has grown by
100x right?
Today, we are moving over 500 terabytes
of data every month between Postgres and
ClickHouse right?
And the other unique pattern is these
are not migrations. These are all users
who are using both Postgres
and ClickHouse together in a continued
and sustained manner, right? What's
interesting is not just the curve

are unique organizations who are using

these are not across one simple

companies, the typical workloads are,

So,

data growth is insane. What I mean by
that is on average, all these companies
grew by 1,000% in data volume over the
last 6 months.
In contrast with the kinds of companies
that I was working with in the past,
where you typically hit that analytics
hurdle once you hit 100 to 500 GB of
data in your Postgres, this point came
late Series B, Series C, which was 18 to
24 months in the life cycle of a
company.
But for AI companies, this wall is being
hit way earlier, 3 to 6 months in their

even probably from day one.
So, the second category of companies
that I wanted to quickly cover are
security and compliance companies,

have lot of streams of data coming in,
and you have how provide signals and

this data is very in line with
clickstream data, right? Like uh which

These are companies that are the Series

POS restaurant data,

are seeing Postgres plus ClickHouse
emerge as a very universal pattern. We
dug into a few uh categories of use

a lot of challenges to overcome when

that you need a team of five to 10
people

the problem is to keep Postgres plus

What I mean is if you don't control the
logs, the wall data on Postgres itself,
you can't really do sub-second
replication to ClickHouse. So, you need
to have a managed offering that we can
control end-to-end.
Right? So, here this is the reference
architecture that we are
having our customers adopt, where you
have Postgres backed by NVMe storage to
provide sub-millisecond tail latency.
You have ClickHouse, which is backed by
object storage like S3, GCS, etc., where
throughput matters more than pure
latency. You have CDC mechanism, which
keeps both these in sync at scale
without having tons of moving pieces.
And the last piece is the application
migration piece that we're trying to
address through PG ClickHouse. I'll

we really believe that this architecture
sets your application up
for the future where scale in data is to

Yeah, coming to the coming to the CDC
piece, right? I've lived and breathed
CDC for the last 3 years, so I'm
very happy to say that like you know, we
have multiple
I like to say this a kitchen sink of
features to solve various problems that
CDC comes up with, right? First thing is
backfilling of data.
Let's say you have your Aurora instance
or RDS instance that has 10 to 100
terabytes of data that you have to move
to ClickHouse.
Moving it through PG dump and PG restore
is going to take forever. So we've done
consistent parallel snapshotting where
we export a snapshot of the data and
move all the tables in parallel to the
destination. This lets you move hundreds
of terabytes in days as opposed to
months right?
The next feature is making sure that we
can keep the replication slot load on
your Postgres instance very low. If
you've ever run CDC, you'll realize that
it's a very fragile process on the
source database. So you have to always
read data from Postgres in a way where
the lag is very minimal. So we
continuously read the slot. We also
decode in-flight transactions even
before they're committed on Postgres and
maintain a state machine so we can roll
back if needed on ClickHouse, right?
And the third piece is coming back to
the problem that I've mentioned earlier
where if we control the wall, we can
move wall decoding out of Postgres,
right? So wall decoding is a very
compute-intensive process that lets you
decode the data and and you know, read
the catalog tables and then decode it
into a stream where you can ingest into
ClickHouse. If you can move this out of
Postgres, your OLTP database Postgres
can serve more transactions, do more
without incurring as much IO as well as
CPU cost, right? So the approach that we
are thinking about taking for this is
once you ship the wall to S3 or any
object store, we have an out-of-process
decoder that can decode this wall and
ingest data into ClickHouse.
Through all this, our goal is to make
replication. So, when your event lands
in Postgres, by the time it's replicated
in ClickHouse, we want to make it under
1 second.
The second problem that we want to solve
is application migrations, right? So, uh
when we
look at the Instacart architecture,
right? You'll see that this doesn't

Apache 2.
It's called PG ClickHouse,

Postgres, right? It analyzes the

critical for an for an FDW or a foreign

gap. I'm not going to promise that every

it'll let you even push down the
subplans to to ClickHouse, right?
This makes your application migration a

everything gets pushed down to
ClickHouse. So, the eventual goal is you
can think of ClickHouse as a read
replica over your Postgres instance, and
you can use this read replica for your
analytical queries, right? So, that's
the goal that we're driving towards.
So, so far, right? To recap, we've

architecture is becoming, the gaps in
this
problem space when you're using Postgres

the way we are trying to address some of

and you know, like the the the promise

architecture that I've kind of shown
here right?

problem that we are trying to solve is
making it really easy to adopt analytics
on your already transactional
application.
Previous attempts at this problem, you
know, broadly called hybrid
transactional and analytics processing
problem, right? Is building something
from the ground up, right? You build a
new database, a new data store that
does both transactions and analytics.
If you look at Postgres and ClickHouse,
both of these make various trade-offs.
Postgres is great for, you know, like
single row inserts, updates, MVCC for
transactions and asset guarantees, but
it's not so good for injection.
ClickHouse is great for injection, but
consistency guarantees and asset are
just not there.
So, if you were to build a new database
around this problem, it will have
different trade-offs that you'll only

migration process.
So, we really think to get both
transactions and analytics to be
state-of-the-art, you need to adopt
best-of-breed platforms for these,
right? Postgres has multiple decades of
research on analytics, so it's great at
Sorry, transactions. So, it's great at
transactions. ClickHouse, same for
analytics. And if you make it really
easy to bundle these two data platforms
together and offer a unified experience,
this really sets up your application for

architecture that that we want our users
to use.
